opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The actuator is really the heart of a humanoid robot. It's the muscle. It decides how strong the robot is, how fast it moves, how efficient it is, how safely it can work around people, and in the end how much the whole system costs. When we looked at what we could buy off the shelf, nothing quite fit what a general-purpose humanoid needs. Most existing actuators were designed for industrial arms bolted to the floor, or they were hobby-grade parts that couldn't survive real work. Neither works for a robot that has to walk, carry loads, recover from bumps, and run all day.

Building our own lets us tune the whole stack together: the motor, the gearbox, the sensing, the electronics, and the control software. That matters a lot. If you want a robot that's compliant enough to be safe around people but strong enough to lift a box, you need tight control over things like torque density, backdrivability, and thermal behavior. You can't get that by stitching together parts from five different suppliers who never talked to each other.

There's also a cost and scale argument. A humanoid has dozens of actuators. If each one is a premium part with a supplier's margin on it, you'll never reach a price where these robots make economic sense in factories, warehouses, or eventually homes. Owning the design means we can design for manufacturability from day one, simplify where it counts, and drive the cost down as volumes grow.

And frankly, it's about the speed of learning. When an actuator fails in the field, or we find a better way to do something, we can iterate in weeks instead of waiting on a vendor's roadmap. In a field moving this fast, that vertical integration compounds. The companies that control their core hardware will learn faster, and in robotics, learning faster is the whole game.

r002.rationale: It says actuators affect how fast the robot moves, but does not identify them as the source of almost all of its speed.

r003.rationale: The response explains that custom actuator design can reduce costs and that without reaching an economically viable price, humanoid robots will not make economic sense.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the simplest answer is that the actuator is the robot. When you look at a humanoid, everything that matters — how strong it is, how fast it moves, how safely it can work next to a person, how long it runs on a battery, and ultimately what it costs — all of that traces back to the actuators. They're the muscles. So if you're buying them off the shelf, you're essentially letting someone else decide what your robot can and can't do.

And the off-the-shelf options were designed for a different world. Most of the motors and gearboxes you can buy were built for industrial arms bolted to a factory floor, or for drones, or for automotive applications. None of those were designed for a machine that needs to walk, balance, pick things up with its hands, and do it all with a limited energy budget on its back. So you end up with components that are too heavy, too stiff, too power-hungry, or just not back-drivable enough to be safe around humans. You can compensate in software to a point, but you're always fighting the hardware.

When we decided to build our own, it wasn't because we wanted the engineering challenge — it's a brutal amount of work. It was because we kept hitting walls. We'd want a joint with a certain torque density, a certain level of compliance, and the ability to sense force precisely enough to do delicate manipulation, and we just couldn't find it. So we started designing the motors, the gearing, the sensing, and the control electronics as one integrated unit, and that let us make trade-offs holistically instead of piece by piece.

The other piece is cost and scale. If you're serious about putting humanoids into the world in real numbers, you can't have a bill of materials where a single actuator costs thousands of dollars and you need dozens of them. Owning the design means we control the supply chain, we can design for manufacturability from day one, and every improvement we make compounds across the whole system rather than waiting for a vendor roadmap.

So I'd say it's a differentiator in the same way that owning your chip design became a differentiator in computing. It's expensive and slow at first, but it's the thing that determines your ceiling. Everyone can run similar AI models eventually. Not everyone will have a body that can actually do what the model wants it to do.

r001.rationale: The response links actuators to the robot’s cost and says they can be expensive, but it does not state that they account for almost all of the robot’s cost.

r002.rationale: It says the robot’s speed, along with its other key capabilities, “traces back to the actuators,” identifying them as the source of its speed.

r003.rationale: It connects actuator design and cost control to producing humanoids “in real numbers,” explaining that affordable actuators and design for manufacturing are needed for scale.

astra-6.text:
Because the actuator is really the fundamental building block of the robot. You can have great software, but what the robot can physically do comes down to how much torque you can produce, how precisely you can control it, how much power it consumes, and how reliably it operates.

If you buy an off-the-shelf actuator, you’re designing around someone else’s tradeoffs. Building it yourself lets you design the hardware around the job you need the robot to do. You can optimize weight, strength, efficiency, and cost together, rather than accepting a fixed package.

And it gives you control over how the design evolves. As you learn from the robot operating in the real world, you can change the actuator itself. That ability to improve the whole system—not just the software—is a really important differentiator.

r003.rationale: It presents actuator design as important and discusses optimizing cost, but does not say getting the design right is necessary for economic viability.

The actuator is really the muscle of the robot. It determines how strong it is, how precisely it moves, how much power it consumes, and how much it costs. If you’re buying that off the shelf, you’re working within somebody else’s design constraints.

Building our own lets us design those things together around what the robot actually needs to do. And when we test the robot and find a limitation, we can go back and change the actuator itself. That control over performance, cost, and the ability to keep improving the design is what makes it an important differentiator.
